# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

</document>
response:
**Sections 1–5 are a valuable correction to the Halden pilot. Sections 6–8 overreach.** The comment ends up making the mirror image of Halden's error: Halden generalised a positive result from self-selected data, and the comment generalises a negative one. Its strongest claim, that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact," is contradicted by the evidence it cites itself.

## What the comment gets right

**Attrition (§1) is the most important new finding.** The working paper said the nine withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons." The microdata show:
- Seven of the nine withdrew *after* the reduced schedule began.
- Six of the nine cited workload or inability to maintain output; only two cited scheduling.

That is a material misstatement in the original paper, and it makes the 61 a sample of survivors. I had flagged the nine withdrawals as excluded before any outcome was measured; the microdata show the problem is worse than that.

**Output measure (§2).** In 19 of the 23 organisations with records, the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based one. Under a simple sign test that is very unlikely to be chance (about p ≈ 0.003, two-sided). So the gap is systematic, and the tone ("we do not suggest bad faith") is appropriate.

**Hours (§3) and revenue (§4).** The arithmetic checks out:

| Figure | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Hours fall, all time-tracked | 34.6 / 40.3 | −14.1% ✓ |
| Hours fall, 17-org subset | 34.8 / 40.4 | −13.9% ✓ |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours | 95.1 / 0.800 | +18.9% ✓ |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours | 98.4 / 0.859 | +14.6% ✓ |
| Record-based output, actual hours | 95.4 / 0.861 | +10.8% ✓ |
| Real revenue | 1.014 / 1.041 | −2.6% ✓ |

**Sectoral claims (§5).** The point that per-hour gains are automatic whenever output stays above 80 is correct. It's the same issue I raised earlier.

## Problems in the strong sections

**1. The abstract claims a correction that was never made.** It says that correcting "the first three" problems (attrition, output, hours) reduces the gain to 10.8%. But Table 2 corrects only output and hours. Attrition is described, not corrected:
- There are no bounds and no imputation.
- There's no worst-case analysis for the nine withdrawals.

The 10.8% is still a survivors-only estimate.

**2. The hours breakdown doesn't add up.** The logs show:
- Days about 0.7 hours longer, over four days, which adds about 2.8 hours.
- About 1.6 hours logged on the day off.

Added to 32 scheduled hours, that gives roughly 36.4 hours. Starting instead from the baseline of about 8.06 hours a day gives roughly 36.6. The reported figure is 34.6, so about two hours are unaccounted for. If the components are right, hours fell even less and the gain is smaller still. Either way, the figures need reconciling.

**3. Record-based output isn't automatically the better measure.** One of the record types listed is **billable hours delivered**. When hours are cut, billable hours fall almost mechanically, whether or not the value delivered per hour changed. In professional services, a record-based index built on billable hours will understate output in any sense that matters.

So part of the −3.8 point gap may come from how output is defined, not from managers rounding toward success. The comment should show the gap separately by record type.

**4. The subsets aren't representative, as the comment acknowledges.** The organisations that kept records and tracked time may differ from the rest. Because of the data note at the end, the corrected estimates are honestly labelled. But the conclusion then ignores that caveat.

**5. The retail evidence is thin.** The 11.2% fall comes from three organisations. Its close match with Varden's −11.4% is suggestive, but it's three data points.

## Where the comment overreaches

**6. "Entirely an artifact" is contradicted by the Varden trial, which the comment cites selectively.** The comment calls Varden's counter-office result "the most reliable finding in the literature." The *same trial* also reports, for case-processing offices:
- randomised assignment, with no self-selection;
- output from administrative records;
- actual hours from timesheets;
- a 7-vs-7 comparison, larger than the counter stratum;
- **+12.5% output per actual hour (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4), at nine months.**

That result removes most of the artifacts the comment identifies:
- **Selection:** removed by randomisation.
- **Manager-reported output:** removed by administrative records.
- **Scheduled-hours denominator:** removed by timesheets.
- **Short-duration novelty:** reduced by the nine-month horizon, though Varden itself notes nine months may still be too short.

Accepting one stratum of a trial as the most reliable evidence while leaving out the other is cherry-picking.

**7. The novelty argument is speculation presented as a conclusion.**
- **The extrapolation rests on two data points.** It takes a linear trend from months three to six and projects zero energy at month ten.
- **Energy isn't productivity.** Self-reported energy can fade while process changes, such as fewer meetings, persist.
- **Novelty isn't a measurement artifact.** A temporary real gain is still a real gain. Grouping "novelty" with "measurement and selection" blurs the distinction.
- **The burden of proof applies to both sides.** "Entirely an artifact" is a positive claim. The comment says itself that six months can't distinguish novelty from a durable effect, which means it can't establish that the gain is novelty either.

**8. The meetings section misdescribes the Varden analysis.**
- **"Selected for analysis after the results were known":** Varden collected meeting data in month six, at managers' request, before the nine-month results.
- **"Fitted to a subgroup":** the seven offices are *all* the treated case-processing offices, not a selected subset.
- **"Should not be cited as a mechanism":** Varden's authors already said a seven-office correlation "cannot establish a mechanism," and they registered a confirmatory test. The comment is rebutting a claim nobody made.

Varden's own numbers also support the meetings hypothesis more than either paper says:
- Actual hours fell about 4.9 hours a week.
- Meeting time was about 3.3 hours lower than in control offices.

That leaves little room for any other explanation. It needs pre-period meeting data to confirm, but it is not "intuitive appeal" alone.

The meetings hypothesis also matters for the novelty argument. If the gain comes from cutting low-value time, there's no particular reason to expect it to fade as enthusiasm declines. The comment dismisses the one mechanism that would make the gain durable, and then concludes the gain is not durable.

**9. The conclusion repeats the error the comment criticises.** It moves from non-random subsets of one self-selected pilot to a claim about "reduced-hours schemes" in general. That is the same overgeneralisation it rightly criticised in "sector-general."

## A defensible conclusion

> The Halden pilot misreported the timing and reasons for attrition, and its headline gain is inflated by manager-reported output and a scheduled-hours denominator. In the subsets where correction is possible, the per-hour gain falls from 23.4% to about 11%, still among survivors. Whether that residual is durable can't be established from six months of data. The best randomised evidence (Varden) suggests per-hour gains of about 12% are real where output isn't tied to presence. Where output is tied to presence, reduced hours reduce output and service.

That keeps everything sound in §§1–5 and drops what the evidence can't support.

## Across the four documents

The first document's §7, "Failures come in pairs," turns out to describe this sequence well:
- **Halden** overclaimed and closed the question too early.
- **This comment**, correcting hard, lands on the other side: it overstates the negative case and finds a flaw in Varden's analysis that isn't there.
- **Varden** comes closest to getting it right.

The first document's tie-breaker was wrong ("the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one"), but its warning about overcorrecting applies here. A careful reply to Halden needed sections 1–5, not 6–8.

If useful, I can draft a response letter from the Halden authors, a referee report on this comment, or a short synthesis of what the three empirical papers jointly support.
